qs.q: What color light is typically emitted when antigens are detected using fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC) as a fluorescent label, such as in direct or indirect immunofluorescence assays?
qs.e: Fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC) is a common fluorophore that, when excited by UV light, emits a characteristic green light.

faq.a: IIF detects a broader range of antibodies and provides pattern information that hints at specific auto‑antibodies, increasing sensitivity.
faq.q: Why is IIF preferred over ELISA for ANA screening?

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with malar rash and arthralgia has a homogeneous ANA pattern on IIF — what does this pattern suggest and what is the next investigative step? — Suggests anti‑DNA/anti‑histone antibodies; order anti‑dsDNA ELISA and complement levels to assess SLE activity.

A patient with chronic diarrhoea tests positive for Giardia by IIF but stool microscopy is negative — how do you interpret this and manage? — IIF confirms exposure; treat with metronidazole and advise hygiene; repeat stool exam if symptoms persist.

In a low‑resource hospital, a clinician wants to screen for SLE but only has IIF slides. What are the limitations they must explain to the patient? — Limited specificity, possible false‑positives, need for confirmatory tests if clinical suspicion remains.

A child from a rural area presents with fever, splenomegaly, and a positive Leishmania IIF — what is the first‑line therapy and why might alternatives be unsuitable? — Liposomal amphotericin B is preferred for safety; antimonials have higher toxicity and resistance in East Africa.

During a rheumatology rotation, you see a speckled ANA pattern. Which specific auto‑antibodies should you consider and what clinical syndromes do they associate with? — Anti‑ENA antibodies (Ro, La, Sm, RNP); associated with Sjögren’s, SLE, mixed connective tissue disease.

A lab reports a weak, granular fluorescence on HEp‑2 cells. How should you convey the result to the ward team? — Report as low‑titer ANA, likely non‑specific; correlate with clinical picture and consider repeat testing if suspicion persists.
ai.title: Indirect Immunofluorescence
ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Indirect immunofluorescence (IIF) is a laboratory technique that uses a labelled secondary antibody to visualise patient antibodies bound to antigens on a slide. It is the reference method for detecting auto‑antibodies (e.g., ANA) and many infectious antibodies in low‑resource settings.

b: Two‑step: patient antibody binding → fluorescent secondary antibody
Requires a dark‑room microscope and a reliable fluorescence source
Interpretation is pattern‑based (homogeneous, speckled, nucleolar, etc.)
sections.p: IIF detects antibodies in patient serum by first incubating the serum with a substrate that contains the target antigen (tissue sections, cells, or pathogen extracts). A fluorochrome‑conjugated anti‑human Ig antibody then binds any patient antibody, producing a fluorescent pattern under a microscope.

IIF is used for autoimmune serology (ANA, anti‑dsDNA, ENA) and for certain infectious diseases where antigen slides are available (e.g., Giardia, Leishmania). In low‑resource hospitals it may replace ELISA when kits are scarce.

t.b: Does the patient have antinuclear antibodies? → Positive fluorescence with a characteristic pattern suggests auto‑immunity; pattern helps narrow the antibody specificity.
Is there evidence of recent Giardia infection? → Fluorescent IgG/IgM bound to trophozoites confirms exposure; if unavailable, stool microscopy or antigen ELISA can be used.
Is visceral leishmaniasis likely? → Positive fluorescence supports diagnosis; if microscopy unavailable, rK39 rapid test is an alternative.

b: Autoimmune positive → refer to rheumatology, start steroids if organ involvement
Leishmania positive → liposomal amphotericin B where feasible; otherwise sodium stibogluconate
sections.p: IIF itself does not treat disease; it guides therapy. Positive ANA may prompt steroids or disease‑modifying agents for SLE, while a positive infectious IIF directs antimicrobial choice.

b: Speckled pattern → anti‑ENA (e.g., Ro, La, Sm)
Nucleolar pattern → anti‑RNA polymerase III, seen in systemic sclerosis
IIF sensitivity > ELISA for ANA, but specificity can be lower
sections.p: Examiners love to test pattern interpretation, limitations of IIF, and alternatives when fluorescence microscopy is not present.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly progressive renal failure in a patient with positive ANA
Acute neurological decline with suspected autoimmune encephalitis and positive IIF
